# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Finds Its Way Up

Water is heavy. This single fact explains most of the engineering behind a municipal water system. A cubic foot of water weighs about 62.4 pounds, and every foot of elevation you lift it costs energy. When you turn on a faucet on the 40th floor of an apartment building, you're drawing on an elaborate system designed to overcome gravity, friction, and the unpredictable rhythms of human demand. Let's trace how that works, using a concrete example.

## The Elevation Head: Gravity Does the First Push

Imagine a city with a reservoir sitting in hills 300 feet above the downtown area. Engineers call this elevation difference "head" — the potential energy stored in water simply by virtue of being high up. Every 2.31 feet of elevation produces roughly 1 pound per square inch (psi) of pressure. So a reservoir 300 feet above a faucet delivers about 130 psi at that faucet, before accounting for friction losses in the pipes.
